item.title: Jupyter: Notebooks and Data Analysis
item.description:
JupyterLab is an interactive notebook, terminal, and data-analysis environment. Pigsty v4.5.0 has two distinct deployment paths:

  • The VIBE module, managed by Ansible and systemd, for the complete v4.5.0 development sandbox.
  • The lightweight standalone app/jupyter Docker Compose template documented here.

app/jupyter is not a default apps inventory entry. Prepare its data directory separately. app.yml -e app=jupyter does not handle directory ownership.

Quick Start 

cd ~/pigsty/app/jupyter
vi .env # change JUPYTER_TOKEN and optionally pin JUPYTER_IMAGE
chmod 600 .env
make dir # create /data/jupyter, owned by 1000:100
make up # docker compose up -d

Generate a strong token with openssl rand -hex 32. The default port is 8888; open http://<host_ip>:8888.

item.title: Dify: AI Workflow Platform
item.description:
Dify is an open-source platform for developing generative AI and LLM applications. It supports agent creation, AI workflows, RAG retrieval, and model management. These features help users build and operate generative AI applications.

Pigsty supports self-hosted Dify with single-command deployment. Critical state resides in externally managed PostgreSQL. You can use pgvector in the same PostgreSQL instance as the vector database to simplify deployment.

  • Quick Start
  • Why Self-Host
  • Installation
  • Configuration
  • Checklist
  • Domain and SSL
  • Upgrading
  • File Backup

The template uses Dify v1.19.0 with plugin daemon v0.6.14-local and sandbox v0.2.15. The previous v1.17.1 template was validated on 2026-10-08 for login, an existing Code workflow, and service connections on Linux amd64 with PostgreSQL 18.6. Dify v1.16 and later handle PostgreSQL 18’s built-in uuidv7() without a local migration patch.

item.title: Odoo: Self-Hosted Open Source ERP
item.description:
Odoo is open-source ERP software with CRM, sales, inventory, and other business applications. The template stays on Odoo Community 19.0 for addon compatibility and uses PostgreSQL 18.

Odoo 19 requires PostgreSQL 13 or later and Python 3.10 or later; the official Docker image provides Python.

Quick Start

On a fresh Linux x86_64 / ARM64 server running a compatible operating system:

curl -fsSL https://repo.pigsty.io/get | bash; cd ~/pigsty
./bootstrap # Install Ansible
./configure -c app/odoo # Generate the Odoo configuration
vi pigsty.yml # Change default passwords
./deploy.yml # Install Pigsty and PostgreSQL
./docker.yml # Install Docker Compose
./app.yml # Initialize the Odoo database and start the web container

Port 8069 is published on all host interfaces by default. Open http://<ip>:8069. The initial application login is admin / admin; change the password at first login.

item.title: Wiki.js: OSS Wiki Software
item.description:
Public Demo: http://wiki.pigsty.cc

The current Compose follows the Wiki.js 2 major-version tag (requarks/wiki:2, resolving to 2.5.317 on 2026-11-06). Stable 2.x releases are maintained in requarks/wiki-v2. Wiki.js 3.0 reached GA in November 2026 under the 3 tag; it is a major rewrite with its own requirements and upgrade procedure, so do not switch an existing 2.x deployment by changing the image tag. Record and verify the actual image version before production upgrades.

TL; DR 

cd ~/pigsty/app/wiki && docker compose up -d

Postgres Preparation 

# postgres://dbuser_wiki:DBUser.Wiki@10.10.10.10:5432/wiki
- { name: wiki, owner: dbuser_wiki, revokeconn: true , comment: wiki the api gateway database }
- { name: dbuser_wiki, password: DBUser.Wiki , pgbouncer: true , roles: [ dbrole_admin ] }
bin/pgsql-user pg-meta dbuser_wiki
bin/pgsql-db pg-meta wiki

Configuration 

services:
 wiki:
 container_name: wiki
 image: requarks/wiki:2
 environment:
 DB_TYPE: postgres
 DB_HOST: 10.10.10.10
 DB_PORT: 5432
 DB_USER: dbuser_wiki
 DB_PASS: DBUser.Wiki
 DB_NAME: wiki
 restart: unless-stopped
 ports:
 - "9002:3000"

Access

  • Default Port for wiki: 9002
infra_portal:
 wiki: { domain: wiki.pigsty.io, endpoint: "127.0.0.1:9002" }
./infra.yml -t nginx_config,nginx_reload -l infra

item.title: Gitea: Self-Hosted Git Service
item.description:
Gitea is a lightweight open-source Git hosting platform.

Pigsty’s app/gitea template uses external PostgreSQL mode by default. Configure the database through GITEA_DB_* values in .env.

Quick Start 

cd ~/pigsty/app/gitea
vi .env # check domain, ports, database settings
make up

Default endpoints:

  • Web: http://git.pigsty or http://<IP>:8889
  • SSH: <IP>:222

Database Preparation 

bin/pgsql-user pg-meta dbuser_gitea
bin/pgsql-db pg-meta gitea

Connection string example:

item.title: PostgREST: Auto-Generated API
item.description:
PostgREST exposes PostgreSQL schemas directly as REST APIs.

Pigsty provides the app/postgrest template as a Pigsty CMDB API example using the read-only dbuser_view role. It publishes port 8884 on all host interfaces by default. Restrict it to loopback as shown below before starting.

Quick Start 

cd ~/pigsty/app/postgrest
vi .env # check DB_URI / DB_SCHEMA / JWT
vi docker-compose.yml

item.title: Kong: API Gateway
item.description:
Kong is an open-source API gateway.

Pigsty’s app/kong template stores configuration in PostgreSQL. For a new empty database, explicitly run the one-time kong-migration initialization job. Normal startup does not run it automatically.

Quick Start

The Admin API is published on all host interfaces by default. Before startup, change its port mapping in docker-compose.yml to "127.0.0.1:${KONG_ADMIN_PORT}:${KONG_ADMIN_PORT}", retaining the two proxy port mappings.

cd ~/pigsty/app/kong
vi .env # check KONG_PG_* and port settings
vi docker-compose.yml # restrict the Admin API host binding
make bootstrap # only when initializing a new empty database
make up

Ports after the change above:

item.title: PGLOG: PostgreSQL Log Analysis Application
item.description:
PGLOG is a sample Pigsty application that uses pglog.sample in MetaDB as its data source. Load logs into this table, then open the related dashboard.

Pigsty provides commands to retrieve CSV logs and load them into the sample table. These shortcuts are available on the meta node by default:

catlog [node=localhost] [date=today] # Print CSV log to stdout
pglog # Load CSVLOG from stdin
pglog12 # Load PG12 format CSVLOG
pglog13 # Load PG13 format CSVLOG
pglog14 # Load PG14 format CSVLOG (=pglog)

catlog | pglog # Analyze current node's log for today
catlog node-1 '2021-07-15' | pglog # Analyze node-1's csvlog for 2021-07-15

Use these links to view the sample log analysis:

item.title: PGWeb: Browser-based PostgreSQL Client
item.description:
PGWeb Client

PGWeb is a browser-based PostgreSQL client. Pigsty includes a small Docker Compose template in app/pgweb. It publishes container port 8081 on host port 8886.

cd ~/pigsty/app/pgweb
vi docker-compose.yml # port mappings are defined in Compose
make up # docker compose up -d

If the portal entry resolves to the Infra node, open http://cli.pigsty. Alternatively, open http://10.10.10.10:8886 directly. The public demo is http://cli.pigsty.io.

item.title: WHO COVID-19 Pandemic Dashboard
item.description:
Covid is a sample applet included with Pigsty. It visualizes the World Health Organization’s official pandemic data.

Browse COVID-19 infections and deaths by country and region, and view global pandemic trends.

Overview

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/pgsty/pigsty-app/tree/master/covid

Online Demo: https://demo.pigsty.io/d/covid

Installation

On the administration node, enter the application directory. Run make to complete installation.

make # Complete all configuration

Other sub-tasks:

item.title: NOAA ISD Global Weather Station Historical Data Query
item.description:
Use the open-source Vonng/isd project to explore weather data in your database.

Use the existing Grafana monitoring system to browse sub-hourly weather data interactively. It covers nearly 30,000 surface stations over the past 120 years.

This is a fully functional data application that can query meteorological observation records from 30,000 global surface weather stations since 1901.

Project URL: https://github.com/Vonng/isd

Online Demo: https://demo.pigsty.io/d/isd-overview

Quick Start

Clone this repository

item.title: Module: Consul
item.description:
Consul is a distributed DCS, KV, DNS, and service registry/discovery component.

Pigsty 1.x used Consul as its high-availability DCS. The current open-source tree no longer includes the Consul role, playbook, or consul_* parameters. You cannot use the inventory from older versions to deploy Consul. Current Pigsty DCS integration is provided by the ETCD module.

item.title: Module: Kubernetes
item.description:
Kubernetes is a production-grade, open-source container orchestration platform. It helps you automate, deploy, scale, and manage containerized applications.

Pigsty has native support for ETCD clusters, which can be used as external etcd for Kubernetes.

The current open-source tree has no kube.yml playbook, Kubernetes role, or kube_* parameters. Pigsty provides software repositories and base-node provisioning. Use kubeadm, SealOS, or another Kubernetes tool for cluster initialization, networking, control-plane management, and upgrades.

SealOS

SealOS is a lightweight, high-performance Kubernetes distribution. It simplifies Kubernetes cluster deployment and management.

item.title: Module: TigerBeetle
item.description:
TigerBeetle is a financial accounting transaction database offering extreme performance and reliability.

Overview

The current open-source tree has no TigerBeetle role or dedicated playbook. It provides only the tigerbeetle installation alias in the node platform package map. Use the official TigerBeetle documentation to initialize and manage the service.

Installation

item.title: Module: DuckDB
item.description:
DuckDB is a high-performance embedded analytical database.

DuckDB is embedded, so it does not require deployment or service management. Install the DuckDB package on the node and use it directly.

Installation

The current Pigsty node platform mapping includes the duckdb package. Install it directly from the Infra repository:

./node.yml -t node_install -e '{"node_repo_modules":"infra","node_packages":["duckdb"]}'

Install with pig:

pig repo add infra -u # add Infra repo
pig install duckdb # install DuckDB package

Resources

item.title: FAQ
item.description:
How mature is the MYSQL module?

This pilot targets simple, low-cost MySQL clusters. Deployment/convergence, HA failover, daily backups, and monitoring/alerts have systematic tests, including fault injection and complete-outage exercises. Destructive recovery remains manual, with procedures. It has no PITR, VIP/DNS access layer, or automatic scaling; its scope is smaller than PGSQL. Before production, validate your requirements and rehearse recovery.

Why is MySQL fixed at 8.4? Can I pick a version?

The fixed platform pins server, client, Shell, Router, and XtraBackup to 8.4 LTS. This keeps compatibility predictable and avoids a broad version test matrix. That tradeoff keeps the pilot simple. Use another tool for other versions or extensive customization.

item.title: Metrics
item.description:
mysqld_exporter supplies raw mysql_ metrics. vmalert derives mysql:ins:* and mysql:cls:* metrics for dashboards and alerts. This page defines those metrics.

files/victoria/rules/mysql.yml provides 68 module recording rules, all listed here. mysql_exporter_up = up{job="mysql"} additionally comes from Infra’s shared liveness recording rules. These recorded metrics do not appear at the raw mysqld_exporter endpoint. mysql_up is the exporter’s database connection probe result.

Common Labels

Metrics carry job=mysql, cls, ins, ip, and topology (standalone or innodb_cluster). Instance-derived metrics retain all identity labels. Cluster metrics aggregate to cls and topology.

item.title: Monitoring
item.description:
MYSQL sends mysqld_exporter metrics to VictoriaMetrics and Journald/Vector error logs to VictoriaLogs. Grafana supplies five dashboards. vmalert loads 68 recording rules and 27 alerts.

Collection Architecture

Each node runs mysqld_exporter on 9104 with least-privilege dbuser_monitor@'127.0.0.1'. Deployment creates a discovery file on the INFRA node:

/infra/targets/mysql/<instance>.yml # e.g. my-test-1.yml

The VictoriaMetrics mysql job reads this directory. mysql_exporter_enabled: false empties the target list. Only mysql-rm.yml removes the file.

item.title: Playbook
item.description:
mysql.yml deploys and adjusts clusters to declared state. Separate mysql-rm.yml retires members or clusters with safeguards. Before every removal, recheck the target, backups, and exact confirmation value.

mysql.yml

Selected clusters follow check → install → bootstrap → access → provision → backup → monitor:

./mysql.yml -l my-test --check # preflight: validate declarations against the live state
./mysql.yml -l my-test # converge one cluster (must select all members)
./mysql.yml # converge every MySQL cluster in the inventory

Usage rules:

item.title: Administration
item.description:
Declare state in the inventory and apply it with the playbook. Most dropped members or AdminAPI drift recover after ./mysql.yml -l <cluster>. Member replacement, physical restore, and complete-outage recovery require the manual procedures below.

Quick Reference

Operation Command
Deploy / converge a cluster ./mysql.yml -l <cluster>
Preflight without changes ./mysql.yml -l <cluster> --check
Local root session mysql --defaults-extra-file=/etc/mysql/pigsty/root.cnf
Inspect MGR topology SELECT MEMBER_HOST,MEMBER_STATE,MEMBER_ROLE FROM performance_schema.replication_group_members;
AdminAPI status dba.getCluster().status() in mysqlsh
Trigger a backup systemctl start mysql-backup (in HA, only the primary runs it)
Retire a secondary ./mysql-rm.yml -l <IP> -e mysql_safeguard=false -e mysql_rm_confirm=<instance>
Retire a whole cluster ./mysql-rm.yml -l <cluster> -e mysql_safeguard=false -e mysql_rm_confirm=<cluster>

Status Checks

Run these commands as root on a cluster member. Only root can read /etc/mysql/pigsty/ credentials. Examples use EL service names. Debian/Ubuntu uses mysql, not mysqld.

item.title: Parameters
item.description:
Deployment exposes 11 parameters; removal adds two protected-operation parameters. Versions, ports, directories, charset, TLS paths, and schedules are fixed. Memory sizing follows node specifications. Use mysql_parameters to change server behavior.

Quick Reference

Parameter Level Default Description
mysql_cluster Cluster required Cluster name and identity
mysql_seq Instance required 1 for standalone; sequential 1..3 for HA
mysql_root_password Cluster DBUser.Root Local root password
mysql_monitor_password Cluster DBUser.Monitor Exporter identity password
mysql_cluster_password Cluster DBUser.Cluster AdminAPI/Router/backup identity password
mysql_databases Cluster [] Additive database declarations
mysql_users Cluster [] Additive user and grant declarations
mysql_parameters Cluster/Instance {} [mysqld] option overrides
mysql_backup_enabled Cluster true Daily full-backup timer
mysql_backup_repo Cluster see below Local backup path and retention
mysql_exporter_enabled Cluster true Exporter and monitoring target

The removal parameters are used by mysql-rm.yml:

item.title: Configuration
item.description:
Declare the cluster in inventory. mysql.yml adjusts live state to match. This page covers topology and configuration blocks. See Parameters for the full reference.

Before You Deploy

  • Manage nodes with NODE. Install the shared CA at /etc/pki/ca.crt through node_ca. MYSQL issues leaf certificates only.
  • Include mysql in repositories with node_repo_modules: node,infra,mysql, or cache packages locally with repo_extra_packages: [mysql].
  • Use supported platforms: x86_64 EL 8/9/10, Debian 12/13, Ubuntu 22/24; or aarch64 EL 9/10.
  • Set production mysql_root_password, mysql_monitor_password, and mysql_cluster_password. Preflight rejects CHANGE_ME placeholders.

Identity

Each cluster is an inventory group with two required identity parameters:

item.title: Module: MYSQL
item.description:
MySQL is a widely used open-source relational database. Pigsty’s MYSQL module installs a fixed native MySQL 8.4 LTS platform on managed nodes. Choose a standalone instance or three-node single-primary InnoDB Cluster with Group Replication. The module manages TLS, backups, monitoring, and lifecycle.

Current status: Pilot module

MYSQL is a supplementary pilot module for a simple, low-cost MySQL cluster. Its scope is smaller than PGSQL. Deployment, convergence, HA failover, daily backups, monitoring, and alerts have systematic tests. Destructive complete-outage recovery and physical restore remain manual. Follow the Administration procedures.

item.title: FAQ
item.description:
How mature is the current KAFKA module?

The v1 baseline provides dynamic KRaft, full-cluster checks, cold start and repair, serial broker admission, and dynamic controller join. It supports retirement of live or dead members and three-command failed-node replacement. It also provides strict rolling restarts, TLS/SCRAM/ACL, declared topics and users, protected credential and certificate rotation, and complete monitoring.

Production requires kafka_security: scram, an odd controller count, and sufficient brokers, RF, and minISR. You must plan capacity, reassignment, balancing, upgrades, backup, restore, and failure exercises. This module does not provide a managed Kafka service. Default plaintext suits only development or trusted isolated networks.

item.title: Metrics
item.description:
Both metric sources use job=kafka. JMX targets have a role label and collect each JVM’s internal state. Protocol targets lack role and collect logical cluster, topic, partition, and consumer-group state through Kafka protocol. Protocol exporters run on the one or two broker-capable nodes with the lowest kafka_seq. Single-broker clusters run one.

JMX is enabled by default and can be disabled per instance with kafka_jmx_exporter_enabled. See Disabling JMX for effects on metrics and discovery.

item.title: Monitoring
item.description:
Kafka monitoring combines metrics, logs, dashboards, and alerts. It covers JVM internals and the Kafka protocol view. You can inspect partitions, ISR, and consumer lag together with JVM state, request queues, and KRaft controller health.

Scrape Architecture

The KAFKA module uses two complementary exporters:

Scrape Surface Service / Method Job Node Scope Main Content
JVM and Kafka internals JMX Exporter Java agent :9404 kafka (with role label) Kafka nodes with JMX enabled (all by default) JVM, broker throughput, replication, request path, KRaft, controller
Kafka protocol view kafka_exporter :9308 kafka (no role label) The one or two broker-capable nodes with the smallest kafka_seq Broker, topic, partition, offset, consumer group, lag
Host resources node_exporter node Managed nodes CPU, memory, disk, network, filesystem
Logs Journald → Vector → VictoriaLogs syslog Kafka nodes with JMX enabled (all by default) Structured, searchable Kafka and exporter logs

On each INFRA node, the role creates one discovery file per instance. JMX and any selected protocol target share that file and kafka scrape job:

item.title: Parameters
item.description:
Source Version Scope

This page follows the current development source snapshot. kafka_jmx_exporter_enabled was added on 2026-09-01. The released v4.5.0 tag does not include it: JMX is always enabled there, and the persistent public parameter count remains 15. The 16 parameters and JMX-disable procedure described here apply to sources containing that change.

KAFKA exposes 16 persistent parameters. The role derives topology, listeners, security, storage subdirectories, replication safety, and exporter placement consistently. Additional persistent variables cannot override these derived settings.

item.title: Configuration
item.description:
KAFKA uses 16 persistent public parameters. The role derives topology, listeners, storage subdirectories, replication safety, authorization, and exporter placement consistently. Start with Quickstart. See Parameters for the field reference.

Plan First, Then Format

kafka_seq becomes KRaft node.id. A new cluster’s bootstrap manifest freezes the random Cluster ID, initial controller identities, security profile, and initial replication policy. After formatting, do not casually change identities, security profile, or controllers. The role checks live state against the manifest and blocks conflicts. It never silently overwrites or reformats data.

item.title: Module: KAFKA
item.description:
Source Version Scope

This page follows the current development source snapshot. kafka_jmx_exporter_enabled was added on 2026-09-01. The released v4.5.0 tag does not include it: JMX is always enabled there, and the persistent public parameter count remains 15. The 16 parameters and JMX-disable procedure described here apply to sources containing that change.

Kafka is a distributed event-streaming platform. Pigsty’s KAFKA module installs Apache Kafka 4.1+ dynamic KRaft clusters on managed nodes from RPM/DEB packages. It manages security, resources, lifecycle, and observability.

item.title: FAQ
item.description:
Deployment

code-server package not found

Make sure that NODE and the repository configuration are ready:

yum repolist # EL
apt-cache policy # Debian/Ubuntu, read-only inspection
./infra.yml -l infra -t repo --check

JupyterLab installation failed

jupyter_venv must exist:

uv venv /data/venv
./vibe.yml -l <host> -t jupyter --check
./vibe.yml -l <host> -t jupyter

Access

Cannot access /code/ or /jupyter/

  1. Check service status
  2. Check port listening
  3. Check Nginx config
systemctl status code-server
systemctl status jupyter
ss -tlnp | grep 8443
ss -tlnp | grep 8888
nginx -t

WebSocket connection fails

Ensure Nginx enables WebSocket (default is enabled). If using custom infra_portal, set websocket: true.

item.title: Monitoring
item.description:
VIBE monitoring mainly uses Claude Code OpenTelemetry data. Code-Server and JupyterLab do not expose Prometheus metrics. Use systemd and logs to check their health.

Claude Code Observability

VIBE writes default OpenTelemetry env vars into ~/.claude/settings.json:

{
 "env": {
 "CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY": "1",
 "OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER": "otlp",
 "OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER": "otlp",
 "OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_METRICS_PROTOCOL": "http/protobuf",
 "OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_LOGS_PROTOCOL": "http/protobuf",
 "OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_METRICS_ENDPOINT": "http://127.0.0.1:8428/opentelemetry/v1/metrics",
 "OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_LOGS_ENDPOINT": "http://127.0.0.1:9428/insert/opentelemetry/v1/logs",
 "OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES": "ip=<host>,job=claude"
 }
}

VIBE merges claude_env with the default settings. Use it to specify API keys or custom endpoints.

item.title: Module: VIBE
item.description:
The VIBE module provides a browser-based development environment. It includes Code-Server, JupyterLab, Node.js, Claude Code, and Codex CLI. It can use JUICE for shared storage and PGSQL for database functions.

VIBE depends on NODE and INFRA:

  • NODE provides base software and Python uv environment
  • INFRA provides Nginx reverse proxy, Grafana and portal entry

Components

Component Description Local Port Access Path
Code-Server VS Code in browser 8443 /code/
JupyterLab Interactive notebooks 8888 /jupyter/
Node.js Runtime and npm - CLI

item.title: FAQ
item.description:
Port Conflicts?

Multiple instances on the same node must use different port values. Example:

juice_instances:
 fs1:
 path: /fs1
 meta: postgres://...
 port: 9567
 fs2:
 path: /fs2
 meta: postgres://...
 port: 9568

Why does changing data not take effect?

Only juicefs format --no-update uses data. This setting does not change the filesystem after creation. To change the backend, migrate the data and reformat manually.

item.title: Monitoring
item.description:
JuiceFS instances expose Prometheus metrics via juicefs mount --metrics. In JUICE, the metrics endpoint listens on 0.0.0.0:<port>. The default port is 9567.

Monitoring Architecture 

JuiceFS Mount (metrics: 0.0.0.0:<port>)
 ↓
VictoriaMetrics (scrape)
 ↓
Grafana Dashboard

If INFRA is deployed, juice_register writes scrape targets to:

/infra/targets/juice/<hostname>.yml

The current source includes the Node JuiceFS dashboard (UID: node-juice). It shows capacity, cache, object-storage, metadata-transaction, and client-resource metrics for JuiceFS mounts on a node.

item.title: Parameters
item.description:
The JUICE module has 2 parameters:

  • juice_cache: shared cache directory
  • juice_instances: instance definition dict

Parameter Overview

Parameter Type Level Description
juice_cache path C JuiceFS shared cache directory
juice_instances dict I JuiceFS instance definition dict (can be empty)

Level: C = cluster level, I = instance level.

Default Parameters

Defined in roles/juice/defaults/main.yml:

#-----------------------------------------------------------------
# JUICE
#-----------------------------------------------------------------
juice_cache: /data/juice
juice_instances: {}

juice_cache

Parameter: juice_cache, type: path, level: C

item.title: Configuration
item.description:
Concepts and Implementation

JuiceFS consists of a metadata engine and data storage. The current version passes meta to juicefs as the metadata engine URL. Production deployments typically use PostgreSQL. Data storage is defined by data options passed to juicefs format.

JUICE module core commands:

# Format (only effective on first creation)
juicefs format --no-update <data> "<meta>" "<name>"

# Mount
juicefs mount <mount_opts> --cache-dir <juice_cache> --metrics 0.0.0.0:<port> <meta> <path>

Notes:

item.title: Module: JUICE
item.description:
JuiceFS is a high-performance, POSIX-compatible distributed filesystem. It can mount object storage or databases as a local filesystem.

The JUICE module depends on NODE for infrastructure and the package repository. It typically uses PGSQL as the metadata engine.

File data can reside in a PostgreSQL jfs_blob table. It can also reside in Silo or S3-compatible object storage from the MINIO module. Monitoring uses VictoriaMetrics from INFRA.

 end

 subgraph JUICE["JUICE"]
 jfs["JuiceFS Mount"]
 end

 subgraph PGSQL["PGSQL"]

 end

 subgraph Object["Object Storage (optional)"]
 s3["Silo / S3"]
 end

 end

 jfs --> meta
 jfs -.->|alternative data backend| blob
 jfs -.->|alternative data backend| s3
 jfs -->|/metrics| vm

 style JUICE fill:#5B9CD5,stroke:#4178a8,color:#fff
 style PGSQL fill:#3E668F,stroke:#2d4a66,color:#fff
 style Object fill:#FCDB72,stroke:#d4b85e,color:#333
 style INFRA fill:#999,stroke:#666,color:#fff

Features

  • PostgreSQL metadata: Metadata stored in PostgreSQL for easy management and backup
  • Multi-instance: One node can mount multiple independent filesystem instances
  • Multiple data backends: PostgreSQL, Silo/MinIO, S3, and more. Metadata and file data remain separate roles.
  • Monitoring integration: Each instance exposes Prometheus / Victoria-format metrics port
  • Simple config: Describe instances with the juice_instances dict

Quick Start

item.title: FAQ
item.description:
Who Can Run Docker Commands?

By default, Pigsty adds two users to the Docker operating system group. One is the management user that runs the playbook: the SSH login user on the target node. The other is the admin user specified by node_admin_username. All users in this group (docker) can manage Docker using the docker CLI command.

To let another user run Docker commands, add that OS user to the docker group:

item.title: Metrics
item.description:
This page retains 122 metric names from a historical DOCKER module scrape. The original scrape time and Docker Engine version were not recorded, so it is not a complete interface for the current version. up and scrape_* come from the collection system, not Docker Engine. Multiple Histogram / Summary sample names occupy separate rows; row counts do not equal metric-family counts.

The current scrape configuration is in roles/infra/templates/victoria/prometheus.yml. It discovers Docker Engine /metrics endpoints from /infra/targets/docker/*.yml and relabels job to node. Query the actual target’s instance with job="node"; do not rely only on job="docker" to determine whether scraping exists. Use the running endpoint for actual names, types, and labels. docker_up comes from Infra’s shared liveness recording rules, matching scrape state by the Docker metrics port. It is not a raw Docker Engine metric.

item.title: Parameters
item.description:
The DOCKER module provides 8 configuration parameters.

Parameter Overview

Use the DOCKER parameter group to deploy and configure the Docker container engine. It controls the enable switch, data directory, storage driver, registry mirrors, and monitoring.

Parameter Type Level Description
docker_enabled bool G/C/I Enable Docker on current node? disabled by default
docker_data path G/C/I Docker data directory, /data/docker by default
docker_storage_driver enum G/C/I Docker storage driver, overlay2 by default
docker_cgroups_driver enum G/C/I Docker cgroup driver: cgroupfs or systemd
docker_registry_mirrors string[] G/C/I Docker registry mirror list
docker_exporter_port port G Docker metrics exporter port, 9323 by default
docker_image string[] G/C/I Docker images to pull, empty list by default
docker_image_cache path G/C/I Docker image cache tarball path, /tmp/docker/*.tgz

You can use the docker.yml playbook to install and enable Docker on nodes.

item.title: Usage
item.description:
Pigsty includes Docker support. Use it to deploy containerized applications quickly.

Getting Started

Docker is an optional module. The docker_enabled parameter controls Docker installation. It is disabled by default.

The docker-ce upstream repository belongs to the infra module. To include Docker packages in the offline repository, set repo_extra_packages to the docker package alias. This alias maps to docker-ce and docker-compose-plugin.

repo_modules: infra,node,pgsql  # <--- Keep infra module (Docker upstream belongs to infra)
repo_extra_packages:
 - pgsql-main
 - docker  # <--- Download Docker (docker-ce + docker-compose-plugin)

After you download Docker, set docker_enabled to true on each target node. Set the other parameters as needed.

item.title: Module: DOCKER
item.description:
Docker is a widely used containerization platform. It provides a standard way to deliver software.

Pigsty provides Docker as an optional module. Pigsty does not require Docker to deploy its components.

Select the Docker software, tool, and application templates that you need. These templates quickly start stateless software in containers to provide extra functions. You can connect these applications to external, highly available database clusters managed by Pigsty.

When you run configure, Pigsty selects suitable upstream repositories and mirror settings from region. For example, it adjusts these settings for networks in mainland China. This improves image download speed and availability.

item.title: FAQ
item.description:
ABORT due to redis_safeguard enabled

This means the Redis instance you are trying to remove has the safeguard enabled. If redis_safeguard is true, redis-rm.yml always refuses to run. The switch does not check whether an instance is running.

First, confirm the exact -l/redis_port target, a recent backup, and the redis_rm_data setting. Then use -e redis_safeguard=false to override the protection and run removal. This switch only disables the guard. It does not verify the target or recovery capability.

item.title: Metrics
item.description:
This page separates raw metrics from scrape endpoints from recorded metrics computed by vmalert. files/victoria/rules/redis.yml defines 96 recording rules. Common examples appear below; the Recording Metric Index lists every name and expression. Query recorded metrics in VictoriaMetrics, not at an exporter’s /metrics endpoint.

Raw metrics vary with software versions, collectors, privileges, instance roles, and runtime state. Historical scrape samples are retained for identifying metrics, not as a complete interface for the current version.

item.title: Monitoring
item.description:
Dashboards

The REDIS module provides 3 monitoring dashboards:

  • Redis Overview: Overview of all Redis clusters
  • Redis Cluster: Details of a single Redis cluster
  • Redis Instance: Details of a single Redis instance

Monitoring

Pigsty provides three monitoring dashboards for the REDIS module:

Redis Overview

Redis Overview: Overview of all Redis clusters/instances

Redis Cluster

Redis Cluster: Details of a single Redis cluster

item.title: Parameters
item.description:
The REDIS module has 22 parameters: 19 for Redis/Valkey deployment and configuration, and 3 for removal.

Parameter Overview

Use the REDIS parameter group to deploy and configure Redis clusters. It controls identity, instance definitions, operating mode, memory, persistence, and monitoring.

Parameter Type Level Description
redis_cluster string C Redis cluster name, required identity parameter
redis_instances dict I Redis instance definitions on this node
redis_node int I Redis node number, unique positive integer in cluster
redis_fs_main path C Redis main data directory, /data/redis by default
redis_exporter_enabled bool C Enable Redis Exporter?
redis_exporter_port port C Redis Exporter listen port
redis_exporter_options string C/I Redis Exporter CLI arguments
redis_type enum G/C Server engine: redis (default) or valkey
redis_mode enum C Redis mode: standalone, cluster, sentinel
redis_conf string C Redis config template, except sentinel
redis_bind_address ip C Redis bind address, defaults to 0.0.0.0; empty uses host IP
redis_max_memory size C/I Max memory for each Redis instance
redis_mem_policy enum C Redis memory eviction policy
redis_password password C Redis password, empty disables password
redis_rdb_save string[] C Redis RDB save directives, empty list disables RDB
redis_aof_enabled bool C Enable Redis AOF?
redis_rename_commands dict C Rename dangerous Redis commands
redis_cluster_replicas int C Replicas per master in Redis native cluster
redis_sentinel_monitor master[] C Master list for Redis Sentinel to monitor

The REDIS_REMOVE parameter group controls Redis instance removal behavior.

item.title: Configuration
item.description:
Concept

The Redis entity model is similar to the PostgreSQL model. It includes Cluster and Instance entities. Here, Cluster does not mean native Redis Cluster mode.

REDIS uses a single-node multi-instance deployment. PGSQL uses a 1:1 deployment. Multiple Redis instances typically share one physical or virtual node to use multiple CPU cores. Thus, the procedures to configure and administer Redis instances differ slightly from PGSQL.

In Pigsty, each Redis node belongs to one cluster. You cannot deploy instances from two different Redis clusters on the same node.

item.title: Module: REDIS
item.description:
REDIS is Pigsty’s Redis-compatible cache module. Select Redis or Valkey with redis_type. The default remains redis. Both engines support primary-replica replication, Sentinel, and native cluster mode. They share configuration paths, instance service names, monitoring, and log entry points.

redis_type: redis  # default; valkey is also supported

The role installs the selected engine and redis-exporter. Instance processes use redis-server / redis-cli or valkey-server / valkey-cli, respectively. A change to redis_type changes packages and binaries. It does not automatically validate data formats, replication topology, or rollback. Rehearse any engine change on an existing cluster. Use the same engine throughout a logical cluster.

item.title: FAQ
item.description:
Which backend does the MINIO module deploy by default?

In v4.5.0, the current source deploys only Silo. The only valid minio_type value is silo. MINIO remains the module name for compatibility. This name does not indicate that the MinIO server is running.

  • Explicitly set minio_type: silo for new clusters.
  • Both minio_type: minio and minio_type: rustfs fail during identity validation.
  • External MinIO, RustFS, or other S3 services can still serve as pgBackRest repositories. The current MINIO role does not manage them.
  • Before upgrading a MinIO cluster managed by an older release, validate the MinIO-to-Silo data compatibility, backup, and rollback procedure.

Why does the Pigsty repository still carry MinIO or RustFS packages?

Upstream MinIO switched to source-only distribution on 2025-10-15. It put the repository in maintenance mode on 2025-12-03 and archived it on 2026-04-25.

item.title: Metrics
item.description:
The MINIO module collects Silo metrics through /minio/metrics/v3. The metric set varies with the server version and enabled features. This page describes the stable interfaces used by current dashboards and alerts. A complete scrape from one version is not a permanent interface contract.

Stable Identity Labels

All object-storage targets use these Pigsty labels:

Label Meaning Example
job Fixed module namespace minio
flavor Actual backend silo
cls minio_cluster identity minio
ins <minio_cluster>-<minio_seq> instance identity minio-1
ip Inventory management address 10.10.10.10
instance Metric target address 10.10.10.10:9000

Queries and recording rules should prefer the stable cls, ins, and ip identity labels.

item.title: Monitoring and Alerting
item.description:
Administration UI

Silo provides an administration UI through minio_admin_port, which defaults to 9001. Access it directly at https://<node-ip>:9001.

Some configuration templates also expose the administration entry point at m.pigsty. Login credentials come from minio_access_key and minio_secret_key.

HTTPS and Certificate Trust

Object storage uses HTTPS certificates issued by the Pigsty CA by default. Browsers and container clients must trust that CA. Do not substitute disabled certificate verification for a correct trust configuration in production.

item.title: Parameters
item.description:
The MINIO module exposes 22 public parameters in two groups:

  • MINIO: 19 parameters for deploying Silo object-storage clusters
  • MINIO_REMOVE: 3 parameters controlling object-storage cluster removal
Architecture Change: Pigsty v3.6+

Since Pigsty v3.6, the minio.yml playbook no longer includes removal functionality. Removal-related parameters have been migrated to the dedicated minio_remove role and minio-rm.yml playbook.

Parameter Overview

The MINIO group configures a Silo object-storage cluster, including identity, storage paths, ports, credentials, and bucket/user provisioning.

item.title: Configuration
item.description:
Before deploying the MINIO module, define a Silo object-storage cluster in the config inventory. The current role requires minio_type: silo and supports these inventory deployment modes:

  • Single-Node Single-Disk: SNSD: Single-node single-disk mode, can use any directory as a data disk, for development, testing, and demo only.
  • Single-Node Multi-Disk: SNMD: Compromise mode, using multiple disks (>=2) on a single server, only when resources are extremely limited.
  • Multi-Node Single-Disk: MNSD: Multiple servers with one independent data drive each, providing compact node-level high availability.
  • Multi-Node Multi-Disk: MNMD: Multi-node multi-disk mode, standard production deployment with the best reliability, but requires multiple servers.

Use SNSD for development and testing. Three-node MNSD provides compact HA with limited resources. Use MNMD for production environments that need more capacity, throughput, and drive redundancy. SNMD handles drive failures within one server but cannot tolerate losing the server.

item.title: Usage
item.description:
First, configure Silo and deploy it with the playbook. Then use this page to access its compatible S3 and mcli interfaces.

Deploy Cluster

First, define a single-node, single-disk object-storage cluster in the config inventory and explicitly pin its engine:

minio: { hosts: { 10.10.10.10: { minio_seq: 1 } }, vars: { minio_cluster: minio, minio_type: silo } }

Then, run the minio.yml playbook provided by Pigsty against the defined group (here minio):

item.title: Module: MINIO
item.description:
MINIO is Pigsty’s compatibility module name for S3-compatible object storage. The current role deploys Silo, and minio_type accepts only silo.

Silo preserves the MinIO S3/Admin APIs, MINIO_* environment variables, disk format, and mcli client interface. It can serve as a PostgreSQL pgBackRest backup repository.

The module name, parameter prefix, and monitoring job retain the MINIO / minio_* namespace. This preserves compatibility with existing inventories and operational entry points.

Important

minio and rustfs are no longer valid minio_type values and fail during identity validation. Before you upgrade a MinIO cluster managed by an older release, complete a backup. Validate MinIO-to-Silo compatibility and rehearse rollback. Do not treat package replacement as an already-accepted data migration. External MinIO, RustFS, or other S3 services can still serve as pgBackRest repositories. The current MINIO role does not manage them.

item.title: FAQ
item.description:
What is etcd’s role in Pigsty?

etcd is a distributed, reliable key-value store for critical system data. Pigsty uses etcd as the DCS (Distributed Config Store) for Patroni. It stores PostgreSQL HA status.

Patroni uses etcd for cluster failure detection, automatic failover, primary-replica switchover, and cluster configuration management.

etcd is critical for PostgreSQL HA. Its own availability requires a reachable majority. Production deployments normally put three or five voting members in independent failure domains.

item.title: Metrics
item.description:
This page separates raw metrics from scrape endpoints from recorded metrics computed by vmalert. As of 2026-10-13, files/victoria/rules/etcd.yml defines 9 recording rules. The table lists each name and expression. Recorded metrics come from rule evaluation and are not found at an exporter’s /metrics endpoint.

Raw metrics vary with software versions, collectors, privileges, instance roles, and runtime state. Historical scrape samples are retained for identifying metrics, not as a complete interface for the current version.

item.title: Monitoring
item.description:
Dashboards

The ETCD module provides one monitoring dashboard: Etcd Overview.

ETCD Overview Dashboard

ETCD Overview: Overview of ETCD cluster

The dashboard shows key ETCD status information. The ETCD Aliveness panel shows the overall cluster service status.

Red bands indicate instance downtime. A blue-gray area below the bands indicates that the cluster is unavailable.

Alert Rules

Pigsty provides five preset alert rules for etcd, defined in files/victoria/rules/etcd.yml:

item.title: Parameters
item.description:
The ETCD module has 13 parameters, divided into two sections:

  • ETCD: 10 parameters for etcd cluster deployment and configuration
  • ETCD_REMOVE: 3 parameters for controlling etcd cluster removal
Architecture Change: Pigsty v3.6+

Since Pigsty v3.6, etcd.yml does not handle removal. Removal parameters belong to the separate etcd_remove role. Since v4.0, Pigsty enables RBAC authentication by default and provides the etcd_root_password parameter.

Parameter Overview

Use the ETCD parameter group to deploy and configure etcd clusters. It controls instance identification, cluster name, data directory, ports, and authentication password.

item.title: Configuration
item.description:
Before deployment, define the etcd cluster in the configuration inventory. Typical choices are:

  • One Node: No HA, suitable for dev, test, demo, or standalone deployments using external S3 backup for PITR
  • Three Nodes: Basic HA, tolerates 1 node failure, suitable for small-medium prod
  • Five Nodes: Better HA, tolerates 2 node failures, suitable for large prod

An etcd cluster can have an even number of members. It has the same failure tolerance as a cluster with one fewer member. The extra member increases deployment and quorum costs. Thus, production clusters usually have one, three, or five members. Clusters with more than five members are uncommon.

item.title: Module: ETCD
item.description:
ETCD is a distributed, reliable key-value store for critical system configuration data.

Pigsty uses etcd as a DCS (Distributed Config Store). It is critical for PostgreSQL high availability and automatic failover.

The ETCD module depends on NODE. The PGSQL module requires ETCD. Install NODE to manage nodes before you install ETCD.

Deploy the ETCD cluster before any PGSQL cluster. For PostgreSQL high availability, patroni and vip-manager depend on etcd. They use it for HA and to bind the L2 VIP to the primary.

item.title: FAQ
item.description:
How to configure NTP service?

NTP is critical for production services. If it is not configured, use public NTP services or Chronyd on the admin node as the time source.

If the nodes already have NTP configured, set node_ntp_enabled to false to preserve that configuration.

Otherwise, if you have Internet access, you can use public NTP services such as pool.ntp.org.

Without Internet access, use the configuration below to synchronize all nodes with the admin node. You can also use another internal NTP service.

item.title: Metrics
item.description:
This page separates raw metrics from scrape endpoints from recorded metrics computed by vmalert. files/victoria/rules/node.yml defines 163 recording rules. Common examples appear below; the Recording Metric Index lists every name and expression. Query recorded metrics in VictoriaMetrics, not at an exporter’s /metrics endpoint.

Raw metrics vary with software versions, collectors, privileges, instance roles, and runtime state. Historical scrape samples are retained for identifying metrics, not as a complete interface for the current version.

item.title: Monitoring
item.description:
The NODE dashboard directory contains 10 monitoring dashboards. Pigsty also provides comprehensive alert rules.

Dashboards

The NODE dashboard directory currently contains 10 dashboards. The JuiceFS and Claude Code dashboards show data only after those components are deployed and emit metrics.

NODE Overview

Shows all host nodes in the current environment.

NODE Cluster

Shows detailed monitoring data for a specific host cluster.

item.title: Parameters
item.description:
The NODE module configures target nodes to the required state. It also adds them to the Pigsty monitoring system.

Parameter Section Description
NODE_ID Node identity parameters
NODE_DNS Node DNS resolution
NODE_PACKAGE Upstream repo & package install
NODE_TUNE Node tuning & kernel features
NODE_SEC Node security configurations
NODE_ADMIN Admin user & SSH keys
NODE_TIME Timezone, NTP, crontab
NODE_VIP Optional L2 VIP for cluster
HAPROXY HAProxy load balancer
NODE_EXPORTER Node monitoring exporter
VECTOR Vector log collector

Parameters Overview

NODE_ID section defines node identity parameters, including node name, cluster name, and whether to borrow identity from PostgreSQL.

item.title: Configuration
item.description:
Pigsty uses the IP address as the unique node identifier. Use the internal IP address on which the database instance listens and provides services.

node-test:
 hosts:
 10.10.10.11: { nodename: node-test-1 }
 10.10.10.12: { nodename: node-test-2 }
 10.10.10.13: { nodename: node-test-3 }
 vars:
 node_cluster: node-test

This address must be a database listening address. It should not be a public IP address. Clients do not have to connect through this address. You can also manage target nodes through SSH tunnels or jump hosts.

item.title: Module: NODE
item.description: Configure nodes to the required state and monitor them. Manage node settings, VIP, HAProxy, and exporters.

item.title: Administration
item.description: This section covers daily administration and operations for Pigsty deployments.

item.title: FAQ
item.description:
What components are included in the INFRA module?

The current infra role directly manages these components:

  • Nginx: Exposes Grafana, VictoriaMetrics (VMUI), Alertmanager, and other WebUIs, and hosts local YUM/APT repositories.
  • DNSMasq: Provides DNS registration and resolution.
  • VictoriaMetrics suite: VictoriaMetrics, VMAlert, VictoriaLogs, and VictoriaTraces.
  • Alertmanager, Blackbox Exporter, and Grafana: Alert dispatch, blackbox probing, and visualization.

infra.yml also runs the CA, repository, NODE, HAProxy, and node-monitoring roles. These configure supporting services such as the self-signed CA, Chronyd, Node Exporter, and Vector on Infra nodes.

item.title: Metrics
item.description:
INFRA monitors VictoriaMetrics, VictoriaLogs, VictoriaTraces, VMAlert, Alertmanager, Grafana, Nginx Exporter, and Blackbox Exporter. Targets come from roles/infra/templates/prometheus/infra.yml.j2; scrape jobs are defined in roles/infra/templates/victoria/prometheus.yml.

Component versions and enabled services affect the raw metric set. This page lists scrape targets, rules, and common metrics for the Victoria stack. See Monitoring System for site-wide counts.

Metric Definitions and Counts

  • Raw metrics: Produced by components or exporters. Read TYPE and HELP at /metrics for their types and meanings.
  • Recorded metrics: Computed from expressions by vmalert and queried in VictoriaMetrics. They have no independent TYPE metadata and cannot all be classified as Counter or Gauge.
  • Scrape status: up and scrape_* are generated by the collection system. up=1 indicates a successful scrape; database and application availability still require functional checks.

Histogram / Summary _bucket, _sum, and _count are different samples of the same metric family. Historical table rows, recording rules, and live time series count different objects and cannot be added together.

item.title: Monitoring
item.description:
This document describes monitoring dashboards and alert rules for the INFRA module in Pigsty.

Dashboards

The current files/grafana/infra directory contains 11 dashboards. The table also includes Pigsty Home from the root directory. See Monitoring System for overall dashboard and rule counts, and Metrics for endpoints and labels.

Dashboard Description

Nginx Instance Nginx metrics and logs
Grafana Instance Grafana metrics and logs

VMAlert Instance Alert rule execution status
Alertmanager Instance Alert aggregation and notifications
VictoriaLogs Instance Log ingestion, querying, and indexing
Logs Instance View log information on a single node

Alert Rules

item.title: Parameters
item.description:
The INFRA module deploys Pigsty infrastructure. This includes the local software repository, Nginx, DNSMasq, VictoriaMetrics, VictoriaLogs, Grafana, Alertmanager, and Blackbox Exporter. It also deploys other monitoring and alerting components.

Pigsty v4.x replaces Prometheus with VictoriaMetrics and Loki with VictoriaLogs for observability.

Section Description
META Pigsty metadata: version, admin IP, region, language, proxy
CA Self-signed CA certificate management
INFRA_ID Infrastructure node identity and service portal
REPO Local software repository configuration
INFRA_PACKAGE Infrastructure node package installation
NGINX Nginx web server and reverse proxy configuration
DNS DNSMasq DNS server configuration
VICTORIA VictoriaMetrics/Logs/Traces observability stack
PROMETHEUS Alertmanager and Blackbox Exporter
GRAFANA Grafana visualization platform configuration

Parameter Overview

META parameters define Pigsty metadata, including version string, admin node IP, repository mirror region, default language, and proxy settings.

item.title: Configuration
item.description:
Configuration Guide

INFRA primarily provides monitoring infrastructure. It is optional for PostgreSQL databases.

INFRA failures typically do not affect PostgreSQL cluster operation. Exceptions apply if you manually configure dependencies on INFRA DNS/NTP services.

One INFRA node is sufficient for most scenarios. For production HA, we recommend 2-3 INFRA nodes.

ETCD, which PostgreSQL HA requires, can share nodes with INFRA to use resources more efficiently.

More than 3 INFRA nodes provide little extra benefit. More ETCD nodes, such as 5, can improve DCS availability.

item.title: Module: INFRA
item.description:
Configuration | Administration | Playbooks | Monitoring | Parameters

Overview

Each Pigsty deployment includes infrastructure components that serve managed nodes and database clusters:

Component Port Description
Nginx 80/443 Web service portal, local repo, and unified entry point
Grafana 3000 Visualization platform for monitoring dashboards and data apps

In Pigsty, the PGSQL module uses some services on INFRA nodes, specifically:

item.title: Repository
item.description:
Pigsty provides supplementary extension repositories. They supply extension packages in addition to those in the official PGDG repository.

YUM Repository

Use this repository with EL 8/9/10 and compatible systems, such as RHEL, Rocky, AlmaLinux, and CentOS.

Add Repository 

# Add GPG public key
curl -fsSL https://repo.pigsty.io/key | sudo tee /etc/pki/rpm-gpg/RPM-GPG-KEY-pigsty >/dev/null

# Add repository configuration
curl -fsSL https://repo.pigsty.io/yum/repo | sudo tee /etc/yum.repos.d/pigsty.repo >/dev/null

# Refresh cache
sudo yum makecache

China Mainland Mirror 

curl -fsSL https://repo.pigsty.cc/key | sudo tee /etc/pki/rpm-gpg/RPM-GPG-KEY-pigsty >/dev/null
curl -fsSL https://repo.pigsty.cc/yum/repo | sudo tee /etc/yum.repos.d/pigsty.repo >/dev/null

Repository URLs

  • International: https://repo.pigsty.io/yum/
  • China: https://repo.pigsty.cc/yum/

APT Repository

Use this repository with Debian 12/13, Ubuntu 22.04/24.04/26.04, and compatible systems.

item.title: FAQ
item.description:
Why can’t my current user use the pg admin alias?

Since Pigsty v4.0, only members of admin on administration nodes can manage global Patroni and PostgreSQL clusters with pg.

The node.yml playbook creates the administration user dba with this permission. To grant the permission to your current user, explicitly add that user to the admin group:

sudo usermod -aG admin <username>

PGSQL Init Fails: Fail to wait for postgres/patroni primary

Several conditions can cause this error. Check the Ansible, systemd, Patroni, and PostgreSQL logs to find the cause.

item.title: Default Extensions
item.description:
During PostgreSQL cluster initialization, Pigsty installs and enables some core extensions by default.

Default Installed Extensions

Pigsty installs these extensions by default through pg_packages:

Extension Description
pg_repack Handle table bloat online, important maintenance tool
wal2json Logical decoding outputs JSON format changes, commonly used in CDC scenarios
pgvector Vector data type and indexes, installed with pgsql-main by default

The default value of pg_extensions is an empty array []. Declare additional extensions as required. For example:

item.title: Remove
item.description:
Extension removal has two levels: drop extension objects from the database, and uninstall packages from the operating system.

Drop Extension Objects

Use DROP EXTENSION to remove extensions from the database:

-- Drop extension
DROP EXTENSION pgvector;

-- If there are dependent objects, cascade delete is required
DROP EXTENSION pgvector CASCADE;

Warning: CASCADE will drop all objects that depend on this extension (tables, functions, views, etc.). Use with caution.

item.title: Update
item.description:
Update extensions at two levels: packages in the operating system, and extension objects in the database.

Update Packages

Use package managers to update extension packages:

# EL systems
sudo yum update pgvector_18*

# Debian/Ubuntu systems
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade postgresql-18-pgvector

Use Pigsty to update packages on multiple nodes:

# Update extension packages for specified cluster
./pgsql.yml -l pg-meta -t pg_extension -e '{"pg_extensions":["pgvector"]}'

# Using pig package manager
pig update pgvector

Update Extension Objects

After you update packages, you may also need to update the extension objects in the database.

item.title: Create
item.description:
After you install extension packages, run CREATE EXTENSION in the database to use their features.

View Available Extensions

After you install extension packages, run these queries to show the available extensions:

-- View all available extensions
SELECT * FROM pg_available_extensions;

-- View specific extension
SELECT * FROM pg_available_extensions WHERE name = 'vector';

-- View enabled extensions
SELECT * FROM pg_extension;

Create Extensions

Use CREATE EXTENSION to enable extensions in the database:

item.title: Config
item.description:
Some extensions require you to preload dynamic libraries or configure parameters before use. This section gives the configuration procedures.

Preload Extensions

After installation, you can enable most extensions with CREATE EXTENSION. Some extensions use PostgreSQL’s Hook mechanism and require preloading.

Set shared_preload_libraries to specify the libraries to preload. A database restart is required to apply the change.

Extensions Requiring Preload

Common extensions that require preloading:

item.title: Download
item.description:
Before you install extensions, make sure that their packages are available from the local repository or an upstream repository.

Default Behavior

By default, Pigsty downloads the base PostgreSQL 18 kernel packages to the local software repository. The default extra download set is repo_extra_packages_default: [ pgsql-main ]. This set includes the PostgreSQL kernel, client, and procedural languages. It also includes basic extension packages such as pg_repack, wal2json, and pgvector.

item.title: Packages
item.description:
Pigsty uses package aliases to simplify extension installation and management.

Package Alias Mechanism

Extensions have different names at different layers:

Layer Example pgvector Example postgis
Extension Name vector postgis, postgis_topology, …
Package Alias pgvector postgis
RPM Package Name pgvector_18 postgis37_18
DEB Package Name postgresql-18-pgvector postgresql-18-postgis-3

Use a package alias to specify an extension without its RPM or DEB package name:

pg_extensions: [ pgvector, postgis, timescaledb ]  # Use package aliases

Pigsty converts each alias to the correct package names for the operating system and PostgreSQL version.

item.title: Introduction
item.description:
Pigsty includes 620 packaged PostgreSQL extensions that are ready to use.

What are Extensions

PostgreSQL extensions add database functionality without changes to the core code. An extension typically consists of three parts:

  • Control file (.control): Required, contains extension metadata
  • SQL scripts (.sql): Optional, defines functions, types, operators, and other database objects
  • Dynamic library (.so): Optional, provides high-performance functionality implemented in C

Extensions can add data types, index methods, functions, and operators to PostgreSQL. They can also add foreign data access, procedural languages, performance monitoring, security auditing, and other features.

item.title: PG Kernels
item.description:
In Pigsty, you can replace the native PostgreSQL kernel with a variant that provides specialized features.

Pigsty supports multiple PostgreSQL kernels and compatibility branches within one operational framework. These kernels provide compatibility layers, multi-master replication, graph queries, MPP warehousing, transparent encryption, and other features.

The level of Pigsty integration differs between kernels. PostgreSQL, Citus, Babelfish, IvorySQL, PolarDB, AgensGraph, and pgEdge have defined templates and configuration procedures. Cloudberry and Greenplum usually use gpsql mode. For their MPP initialization and scale-out operations, upstream tools remain the preferred method.

item.title: Param Templates
item.description:
Pigsty provides four preset Patroni/PostgreSQL config templates optimized for different workloads:

Template CPU Cores Use Case Characteristics
/docs/pgsql/template/oltp.yml 4-128C OLTP transactions High concurrency, low latency
/docs/pgsql/template/olap.yml 4-128C OLAP analytics Large queries, high parallelism
/docs/pgsql/template/crit.yml 4-128C Consistency-first Consistency-first, detailed auditing
/docs/pgsql/template/tiny.yml 1-3C Tiny instances Resource-constrained envs

Use pg_conf to select a template. The default is /docs/pgsql/template/oltp.yml.

The database tuning template pg_conf should be paired with the OS tuning template node_tune.

item.title: Bind a L2 VIP to PostgreSQL Primary with VIP-Manager
item.description:
If all cluster nodes share one L2 network, you can optionally define an L2 VIP for the PostgreSQL cluster.

The VIP uses Master-Backup mode. It always points to the node that runs the cluster primary instance.

VIP-Manager manages the VIP. It reads the Leader Key that Patroni writes to DCS (etcd) to determine whether the local node is primary.

Enable VIP

To enable VIP for a cluster, set pg_vip_enabled to true at cluster level. You can also enable it globally.

item.title: Extensions
item.description:
Pigsty provides 620 packaged extensions that are ready to use. The extensions cover 16 major categories, including time-series, geospatial, vector, full-text search, analytics, and feature enhancements.

To use extensions in Pigsty, complete four steps: Download, Install, Config/Load, and Create.

pg-meta:
 hosts: { 10.10.10.10: { pg_seq: 1, pg_role: primary } }
 vars:
 pg_cluster: pg-meta
 pg_databases:
 - name: meta
 extensions: [ postgis, timescaledb, vector ]  # Create: Create extensions in database
 pg_libs: 'timescaledb, pg_stat_statements, auto_explain' # Config: Preload extension libraries
 pg_extensions: [ postgis, timescaledb, pgvector ]  # Install: Install extension packages

item.title: Parameters
item.description:
Install PGSQL only on nodes that Pigsty manages through the NODE module. The deployment also needs an available ETCD cluster to store cluster metadata.

Install PGSQL on one node to create a standalone server, which is a primary instance. Install it on additional nodes to create read replicas that provide standby capacity and read-only access. You can create offline instances for ETL, OLAP, and interactive queries. Use synchronous standby and quorum commit for stronger data consistency. Use standby clusters and delayed clusters to respond quickly to data loss from human error or software defects.

item.title: Metrics
item.description:
This page separates raw metrics from scrape endpoints from recorded metrics computed by vmalert. files/victoria/rules/pgsql.yml defines 402 recording rules. Common examples appear below; the Recording Metric Index lists every name and expression. Query recorded metrics in VictoriaMetrics, not at an exporter’s /metrics endpoint.

Raw metrics vary with software versions, collectors, privileges, instance roles, and runtime state. Historical scrape samples are retained for identifying metrics, not as a complete interface for the current version.

item.title: Dashboard
item.description:
Pigsty provides Grafana monitoring dashboards for PostgreSQL: Demo & Gallery.

The current source provides 31 PostgreSQL-related dashboards. It includes 29 PostgreSQL / PGCAT dashboards under files/grafana/pgsql and two PGLOG dashboards under files/grafana/app. The hierarchy has four categories: Overview, Cluster, Instance, and Database. The data source categories are PGSQL, PGCAT, and PGLOG.

Overview

Overview Cluster Instance Database
PGSQL Overview PGSQL Cluster PGSQL Instance PGSQL Database
PGSQL Alert PGRDS Cluster PGRDS Instance PGCAT Database
PGSQL Shard PGSQL Activity PGCAT Instance PGSQL Tables
PGSQL Replication PGSQL Persist PGSQL Table
PGSQL Service PGSQL Proxy PGCAT Table
PGSQL Databases PGSQL Pgbouncer PGSQL Query
PGSQL Patroni PGSQL Session PGCAT Query
PGSQL PITR PGSQL Xacts PGCAT Locks
PGSQL Exporter PGCAT Schema

Overview

item.title: Monitoring
item.description:
This page describes the Pigsty monitoring architecture, including metrics, logs, and target management. It also explains how to monitor existing PostgreSQL clusters and remote RDS services.

Monitoring Overview

Pigsty uses these observability components for PostgreSQL monitoring:

  • Grafana displays metrics and provides PostgreSQL data sources.
  • VictoriaMetrics collects PostgreSQL, Pgbouncer, Patroni, HAProxy, and node metrics.
  • VictoriaLogs stores PostgreSQL, Pgbouncer, Patroni, pgBackRest, and host component logs.
  • Included Grafana dashboards cover all PostgreSQL operations. The set changes with each release. Use the live demo and this page’s dashboard links.

Metrics

item.title: Reference
item.description: Parameters and reference documentation

item.title: Data Migration
item.description:
Pigsty includes the pgsql-migration.yml playbook for online database migration with logical replication.

The generated automation scripts can reduce application downtime to a few seconds. Logical replication requires PostgreSQL 10 or later.

If the permitted downtime is sufficient, you can use pg_dump | psql for offline migration.

Defining Migration Tasks

To use the online migration playbook, create a definition file that describes the migration task.

Refer to the task definition file example: files/migration/pg-meta.yml.

item.title: Authentication / HBA
item.description:
Detailed explanation of Host-Based Authentication (HBA) in Pigsty.

Authentication supports Access Control and Default Privileges. PostgreSQL supports several authentication methods.

This page describes HBA, or Host-Based Authentication. HBA rules specify which users can access each database, from which locations, and with which authentication methods.

Client Authentication

Users must authenticate before they connect to a PostgreSQL database. By default, they use a password.

You can put the password in the connection string, but this is not secure. Alternatively, use the PGPASSWORD environment variable or a .pgpass file. For details, see psql and PostgreSQL Connection Strings.

item.title: Database
item.description:
In this context, Database refers to the logical object created using the SQL command CREATE DATABASE within a database cluster.

A PostgreSQL server can serve multiple databases at the same time. In Pigsty, define the required databases in the cluster configuration.

Pigsty customizes the default template database, template1. It creates default schemas, installs default extensions, and configures default privileges. New databases inherit these settings from template1 by default.

By default, Pigsty adds each business database to the Pgbouncer connection pool with a 1:1 mapping. pg_exporter automatically discovers all business databases and monitors their objects.

item.title: User / Role
item.description:
In this context, users refer to logical objects within a database cluster created using the SQL commands CREATE USER/ROLE.

In PostgreSQL, users belong to the database cluster, rather than a specific database. Create business users before you create business databases.

Defining Users

Pigsty defines roles and users in database clusters through two configuration parameters:

  • pg_default_roles: Defines globally unified roles and users
  • pg_users: Defines business users and roles at the database cluster level

The first parameter defines roles and users shared across the environment. The second defines business roles and users for individual clusters. Both use arrays of user definition objects.

item.title: Backup & Restore
item.description:
Pigsty uses pgBackRest for PostgreSQL backups. It supports full, differential, and incremental backups, parallel processing, encryption, and Silo/S3 object storage. By default, Pigsty configures backup and WAL archiving for every PGSQL cluster.

This chapter is the operational manual for backup configuration, management, recovery, and drills. For design concepts and tradeoffs, see Point-in-Time Recovery.

All backup and recovery operations call pgBackRest. Pigsty provides these wrapper layers:

Layer Interface Form Scope
Cluster orchestration pg_pitr + pgsql-pitr.yml Ansible playbook HA, etcd, and multi-node recovery
Instance orchestration pig pitr CLI Local-node recovery without the admin node
Command primitives pig pb, pb, and pg-backup pgBackRest wrappers Backup, inspection, expiry, and unmanaged restore
Engine pgbackrest Native CLI Underlying backup, archive, and restore engine
Section Content
Mechanism Stanzas, repositories, retention, timelines, and Pigsty wrapper mapping
Policy Scheduling, recovery windows, and storage planning
Repository Local, Silo, and external S3 repositories; encryption, versioning, and locking
Administration Backup commands, inspection, expiration, and stanza management
Restore Recovery targets, staged PITR, and complete parameter reference
Clone Restore production history into another cluster and perform drills
Tutorial A sandbox restore using pgBackRest primitives
Disclaimer

Pigsty makes every effort to provide a reliable PITR solution. It accepts no liability for data loss caused by restore operations. If you need assistance, consider professional services.

item.title: Administration
item.description: Database administration and operation tasks

item.title: Access Control
item.description:
Pigsty access-control documentation is organized by purpose:

  • Access Control Concepts: role model, default privileges, database ACLs, and instance-isolation boundaries.
  • Access Control Configuration: pg_default_roles, pg_users, pg_default_privileges, and related parameters.
  • Authentication: HBA, SCRAM, certificate authentication, and credential management.
  • HBA Configuration: PostgreSQL and PgBouncer rule syntax.
  • User Management: create, update, and remove users in an existing cluster.

dbrole_offline provides independent read-only object privileges. It does not restrict instance scope automatically. To allow access only on offline instances, set role: offline explicitly on the corresponding HBA rule. Verify the generated pg_hba.conf on both online and offline instances.

item.title: Service / Access
item.description:
Separate read and write operations, route traffic correctly, and deliver PostgreSQL cluster capabilities reliably.

A service exposes database cluster capabilities to clients. It hides the details of the underlying cluster.

Services provide stable access in production, including after automatic failover in high-availability clusters. Single-node users usually do not need services.

Single-Node Users

Services are intended for production environments. Personal users and single-node clusters can connect directly through an instance name or IP address.

item.title: PostgreSQL Security
item.description:
PostgreSQL security combines authentication, authorization, network boundaries, encrypted communication, data protection, and operating procedures. Pigsty provides configuration parameters for these mechanisms. Operators must still harden, verify, and audit the deployment for its environment.

Concepts and Boundaries

Topic Content
Security and Compliance Default state, capability boundaries, and hardening path
Authentication HBA, SCRAM, certificate authentication, and credential management
Access Control Built-in roles, default privileges, database ACLs, and instance-access boundaries
Encrypted Communication CA, TLS, server authentication, and certificate rotation
Data Security Page checksums, replication, backup, PITR, audit, and logging
Compliance Launch checks, control mappings, and evidence requirements

Configuration Reference

  • HBA Configuration: declare PostgreSQL and PgBouncer authentication rules.
  • Access Control Configuration: configure default roles, application users, object privileges, and database ACLs.
  • User Configuration: define user attributes, role membership, and connection-pool options.
  • CRIT Parameter Template: critical parameters for synchronous replication, checksums, logging, and watchdog.

Administration and Verification

  • User Management: create, update, and remove users.
  • HBA Management: refresh rules, inspect effective configuration, and troubleshoot authentication.
  • Security Considerations: production hardening and acceptance checklist.
  • Security Recommendations: minimum password, network, and file checks before installation.

The inventory describes the required state. Acceptance checks should inspect HBA, certificates, listening ports, and sensitive files on running nodes. They should also verify effective roles and privileges through PostgreSQL catalogs.

item.title: Service/Access
item.description:
Split read and write operations, route traffic correctly, and reliably deliver PostgreSQL cluster capabilities.

A service exposes database cluster capabilities to clients. It hides the details of the underlying cluster.

Services provide stable access in production, including after automatic failover in high-availability clusters. Single-node users usually do not need services.

Personal User

Services are intended for production environments. Personal users and single-node clusters can connect directly through an instance name or IP address.

item.title: Configuration
item.description:
Pigsty uses configuration to control PostgreSQL behavior. This configuration combines inventory files in ~/pigsty/conf/*.yml with PGSQL parameters. After you write the configuration, you can reproduce a customized cluster in a few minutes. The configuration includes instances, users, databases, access control, extensions, and tuning policies.

Configuration Entry

  1. Prepare Inventory: Copy a pigsty/conf/*.yml template or write an Ansible inventory. Put cluster groups (all.children.<cls>.hosts) and global variables (all.vars) in the same file.
  2. Define Parameters: Override the required PGSQL parameters in vars. The override order is global → cluster → host. The last applicable setting determines the value.
  3. Generate and Apply Inventory: ./configure -c <conf> generates pigsty.yml from the selected template. Then run ./pgsql.yml -l <cls> or bin/pgsql-add <cls> against uninitialized targets to deploy services. Use the corresponding dedicated playbooks or tags for maintenance of initialized clusters.

The PostgreSQL kernel example inventory, conf/pgsql.yml, provides a minimal example. It defines one pg-meta cluster, global pg_version: 18, and a few application users and databases. You can add more clusters to this configuration.

item.title: demo/wool
item.description:
demo/wool targets small cloud instances in China. It defaults to region: china, PostgreSQL 18, and the tiny tuning profiles.

Overview

  • Config Name: demo/wool
  • Node Count: Single node
  • Suggested Size: Approximately 2 vCPU / 2 GB for testing
  • Related: meta, slim
./configure -c demo/wool [-i <private_ip>]

Content

Source: pigsty/conf/demo/wool.yml

---
#==============================================================#
# File : wool.yml
# Desc : Pigsty Aliyun ECS 羊毛机配置文件
# Ctime : 2020-11-09
# Mtime : 2025-12-12
# Docs : https://pigsty.io/docs/conf
# License : Apache-2.0 @ https://pigsty.io/docs/about/license/
# Copyright : 2018-2026 Ruohang Feng / Vonng (rh@vonng.com)
#==============================================================#

all:
 children:

 # 建议使用操作系统： RockyLinux 9.4
 # 这里的 10.10.10.10 都应该是你 ECS 的内网 IP 地址，用于安装 Infra/Etcd 模块
 infra: { hosts: { 10.10.10.10: { infra_seq: 1 } } }
 etcd: { hosts: { 10.10.10.10: { etcd_seq: 1 } }, vars: { etcd_cluster: etcd } }

 # 定义一个单节点的 PostgreSQL 数据库实例
 pg-meta:
 hosts: { 10.10.10.10: { pg_seq: 1, pg_role: primary } }
 vars:
 pg_cluster: pg-meta
 pg_databases:
 - { name: meta ,baseline: cmdb.sql ,schemas: [ pigsty ] }
 pg_users: # 最好把这里的两个样例用户的密码也修改一下
 - { name: dbuser_meta ,password: DBUser.Meta ,roles: [ dbrole_admin ] }
 - { name: dbuser_view ,password: DBUser.Viewer ,roles: [ dbrole_readonly ] }
 pg_conf: tiny.yml  # 2C/2G 的云服务器，使用微型数据库配置模板
 node_tune: tiny  # 2C/2G 的云服务器，使用微型主机节点参数优化模板
 pgbackrest_enabled: false # 这么点磁盘空间，就别搞数据库物理备份了
 pg_version: 18 # 用 PostgreSQL 18

 vars:
 version: v4.5.0  # pigsty version string
 region: china
 admin_ip: 10.10.10.10 # 这个 IP 地址应该是你 ECS 的内网IP地址
 infra_portal: # 如果你有自己的 DNS 域名，这里面的域名后缀 pigsty 换成你自己的 DNS 域名
 home : { domain: i.pigsty }  # default domain name
 minio: { domain: m.pigsty ,endpoint: "${admin_ip}:9001" ,scheme: https ,websocket: true }
 postgrest: { domain: api.pigsty ,endpoint: "127.0.0.1:8884" }
 pgadmin: { domain: adm.pigsty ,endpoint: "127.0.0.1:8885" }
 pgweb: { domain: cli.pigsty ,endpoint: "127.0.0.1:8886" }
 bytebase: { domain: ddl.pigsty ,endpoint: "127.0.0.1:8887" ,websocket: true }
 jupyter: { domain: lab.pigsty ,endpoint: "127.0.0.1:8888", websocket: true }
 gitea: { domain: git.pigsty ,endpoint: "127.0.0.1:8889" }
 wiki: { domain: wiki.pigsty ,endpoint: "127.0.0.1:9002" }
 noco: { domain: noco.pigsty ,endpoint: "127.0.0.1:9003" }
 supa: { domain: supa.pigsty ,endpoint: "10.10.10.10:8000", websocket: true }

 # 把这里的密码都改掉！你也不想别人随便来串门对吧！
 #----------------------------------------------#
 # PASSWORD : https://pigsty.io/docs/setup/security/
 #----------------------------------------------#
 grafana_admin_password: pigsty
 grafana_view_password: DBUser.Viewer
 pg_admin_password: DBUser.DBA
 pg_monitor_password: DBUser.Monitor
 pg_replication_password: DBUser.Replicator
 patroni_password: Patroni.API
 haproxy_admin_password: pigsty
 minio_secret_key: S3User.MinIO
 etcd_root_password: Etcd.Root
...

Explanation

  • Explicitly sets pg_conf: tiny.yml and node_tune: tiny on pg-meta
  • Expects 10.10.10.10 to be replaced by the cloud instance’s private IP
  • Disables pgBackRest by default to reduce disk usage on a small test host
  • Includes several example portal domains

This template reduces resource use by disabling backups. It is suitable only for temporary testing.

item.title: demo/saas
item.description:
demo/saas is a legacy single-node example with many features. It includes predefined business users, databases, and application entrypoints. It demonstrates how to combine PostgreSQL, Silo, Redis, Docker, and the portal.

  • Modules: INFRA, ETCD, MINIO, PGSQL, REDIS, DOCKER

./configure -c demo/saas [-i <primary_ip>]

all:

 - {name: dbuser_view ,password: DBUser.Viewer ,pgbouncer: true ,roles: [dbrole_readonly] ,comment: read-only viewer for meta database }

 pg_databases:
 - {name: meta ,baseline: cmdb.sql ,comment: pigsty meta database ,schemas: [pigsty] ,extensions: [{name: vector},{name: postgis},{name: timescaledb}]}

 - {name: bytebase ,owner: dbuser_bytebase ,revokeconn: true ,comment: bytebase primary database }

 #- {name: odoo ,owner: dbuser_odoo ,revokeconn: true ,comment: odoo main database }
 pg_hba_rules:
 - {user: dbuser_view , db: all ,addr: infra ,auth: pwd ,title: 'allow grafana dashboard access cmdb from infra nodes'}
 pg_libs: 'timescaledb,pg_stat_statements, auto_explain' # add timescaledb to shared_preload_libraries
 node_crontab: # make one full backup 1 am everyday
 - '00 01 * * * /pg/bin/pg-backup full'

 postgrest : { domain: api.pigsty ,endpoint: "127.0.0.1:8884" }
 pgadmin : { domain: adm.pigsty ,endpoint: "127.0.0.1:8885" }
 pgweb : { domain: cli.pigsty ,endpoint: "127.0.0.1:8886" }
 bytebase : { domain: ddl.pigsty ,endpoint: "127.0.0.1:8887" }
